Based on the provided passages, the treatment for an asset discarded as per the Income Tax Act is as follows:

If an asset is discarded by a business without selling it, the scrap value of the asset can be reduced from the block of assets in the previous year in which the asset was discarded, as per Section 43(6) of the Income Tax Act.

The block concept applies to all assets falling within the same class and subject to the same rate of depreciation, and any alterations to the value of the block must be made in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV D of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

If the assessee is entitled to claim depreciation on the residual value of a discarded asset, they can do so even if the asset is not used for business or professional purposes in the current year or subsequent years, as per Section 50(1) of the Income Tax Act.

Therefore, the treatment for an asset discarded as per the Income Tax Act is to reduce the scrap value from the block of assets in the previous year, follow the block concept for calculating depreciation, and claim depreciation on the residual value of the discarded asset even if it is not used for business or professional purposes.

To wash wine glasses properly, follow these steps:
Lay a towel in the sink and fill it with hot water.
Wash one wine glass at a time to avoid damage.
Use a small amount of mild detergent and apply it only to the bottom of the glass and around the rim.
Scrub the inside of the glass with a stemware brush that has soft-foam bristles.
Rinse the glass thoroughly with hot water.
If there is stubborn wine residue, dissolve a small amount of baking soda in hot water and let it stand in the glass for a few minutes.
Gently scrub the glass again with the stemware brush.
Rinse the glass once more with hot water.
Dry the wine glasses with a smooth lint-free cloth, such as a microfiber or flour sack towel.
Make sure to dry them completely to avoid any stains or spots.

Based on the provided passages, the main difference between an adverb clause and an adjective clause is as follows:
An adverb clause is a dependent clause that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb.
It is introduced by subordinate conjunctions such as after
although, as, as if, before, because, if, since, so that, than, though, unless, until, when, where, and while.
An adjective clause, on the other hand, is a dependent clause that modifies a noun or a pronoun.
It is introduced by a relative pronoun (who, whose, him, her, it, that) or a subordinate conjunction (when and where).
In summary
both adverb clauses and adjective clauses are dependent clauses, they differ in their function and the words that introduce them.
Adverb clauses modify verbs, adjectives, or another adverbs
adjective clauses modify nouns or pronouns.

Based on the given passages, here's how twins happen:
Monozygotic (identical) twins occur when the split takes place after the ninth day after fertilization, specifically within 8 days of fertilization.
This results in two embryos developing from one zygote.
Dizygotic (fraternal) twins, on the other hand, occur when two different eggs are fertilized by separate sperm cells.
The likelihood of having dizygotic twins increases for women who are of West African descent (especially Yoruba), between the ages of 30 and 40 years old, and have had several previous pregnancies.
Therefore, twins can occur either through the splitting of one zygote (monozygotic) or the fertilization of two separate eggs (dizygotic).

Based on the given passages, here's how E-Z Pass charges work:
When you sign up for E-Z Pass, a certain amount (specifically $100 for the EZ-Tag or $25 for the TX-Tag) is charged to your credit card to establish a balance.
As you drive through tolls, the system deducts the toll amounts from your balance until it reaches a certain threshold ($10 for the TX-Tag).
When your balance falls below this threshold, your credit card is automatically charged again to increase your balance.
This process continues until your account is closed or your balance is depleted.

Based on the given passages, here are the differences and similarities between red and white blood cells:

Differences:
Function: Red blood cells are responsible for delivering oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues
white blood cells are part of the immune system and help combat diseases and infections.
Structure: Red blood cells have a unique biconcave disk shape that allows them to maximize their surface area for gas exchange
white blood cells have a irregular, amoeba-like shape.
Similarities:
Formation: Both red and white blood cells are formed from pluripotent stem cells in the red bone marrow.
Presence in circulatory system: Both red and white blood cells are found in the circulatory system and can be carried by blood from one part of the body to another.
Cellular components: Both red and white blood cells have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.
Therefore
red and white blood cells have some similarities in terms of their formation and presence in the circulatory system, they differ in their function and structure.
